4609d17389d8ad96e82d.text: Bias refers to a tendency to lean in a particular direction or side. It is a

6d417075b61e172cb506.text: disposition to be in favor of or against one thing, person, or group. It is having a concept or thought in a way considered to be unfair. Biases can be learned or acquired implicitly within cultural contexts. A person may develop biases toward or against an individual, an ethnic group, a sexual or gender identity or preference, a nation, a religion, social class, political views, ideologies, physical attributes, abilities, and disabilities.

b662dab445ccd35d8d16.text: To be biased means to lack a neutral perspective on a specific matter. It means one-sided, lacking a balanced viewpoint, or someone not having an open mind. When people are biased towards something, they lean favorably towards it and think positively of it. On the other hand, when they are biased against something, they lean negatively against it and think poorly of it.

6fe9c35be4ae2b56ba6f.text: Prejudice is an irrational or incorrect attitude towards an individual or a person

a61548a7647fdcff46e3.text: based solely on their social group membership. The word is often used to denote preconceived, usually unfavorable feelings, towards people or a person because of their age, gender, sex, disability, race/ethnicity, nationality, education, occupation, social class, beliefs, religion, values, political views, sexuality, language, beauty, criminality, affiliation or other personal characteristics.

8aca51826e5bbc754e2c.text: Moreover, it is a positive or negative evaluation of another person based on

8a95aae03c8e5df2f4fd.text: their apparent group membership or what people think they belong. Prejudice can also refer to unfounded or unsupported beliefs or an idea or opinion that disregards basic

21a5f8184db4f1f0777d.text: facts. It is similar to ignorance or a lack of knowledge, experience, or education.

e67b67c5f5ebd086bc01.text: In contemporary times, many get the information they need from viewing   materials, like news programs, educational videos, among others. With the vast, often   conflicting, amount of information offered by these materials, people must know how   to evaluate them to avoid misinformation.      Evaluation is a skill founded on one's capacity to understand the content. Before   we can form a judgment about the quality and value of the material, we must have a   solid grasp of what it conveys. Here are the steps on how you can get a sense of the   materials you view.       FIRST, identify the topic – the subject of the material. Your strategy for topic   identification is to ask yourself the question, "What is this about?" Sometimes,   you can spot the topic by looking for a word or two that repeat. Usually, you   can state it in a few words.

e7d56aa6a4ce614ea745.text:  SECOND, look for the main idea. Stated at the beginning, in the middle, or at the end, it is the essential piece of information the author wants you to know. It is either explicit (directly stated) or implicit (indirectly stated).

b78d18c4319bac7e57d7.text:  THIRD, find the supporting details. They are facts, statements, and examples- -specifics that clarify, illuminate, explain, describe, expand and illustrate the main idea.

1a3807782325bbb5ca66.text:  The process of determining supporting details is as follows:

22910f5544b23b92ded1.text: 1. Decide which details help to further the storyline. 2. Decide which details help you to understand the main idea. 3. Answer question raised by the main idea (who, what, when, why, or how).

0f62b2a5e90cae9a1a35.text: Let us consider the paragraph below.

32d9a55e996a1d472a61.text: The movie Outbreak was an epic, semi-realistic film in 1995. It is about a small, quarantined town in California, where the residents fall victim to an Ebola-like virus that stems from Capuchin monkeys in Zaire. When the movie was released, there was also an Ebola virus in Zaire, which made the movie quite scary for some viewers in the real world. It is an entertaining disaster movie that poses the horrific idea that diseases lurk in nature, and they could strike humanity at any time.

09fb554963695b62b4bb.text: 1. The subject or the topic, or the one being discussed in the text, is the movie "Outbreak." 2. The main idea is presented in the last sentence:

4195cfd6d8718222842a.text: It is an entertaining disaster movie that poses the horrible idea that diseases

f90b577b838b20bff39d.text: lurk in nature, and they could strike humanity at any time.

5262f3fafade80a37436.text: Notice that the main idea is explicitly stated in the last statement. It tells us the kind of movie Outbreak is and the central idea it conveys. 3. All the other sentences in the paragraph lead you to the stated main idea. They

8eb324e13c9d7da95874.text: help you grasp the meaning of the material.

be3ac54ea752de598fcb.text: Agreeing or disagreeing with a material viewed shows our stand on a particular

dc654bd503e90ba10bac.text: issue. It indicates whether we have the same (agreement) or a different idea (disagreement) as the one presented. There are expressions we can use to show either agreement or disagreement, such as:

rows:  I agree with you 100 percent.  I couldn't agree with you more.  That's so true.  That's for sure.  (slang) Tell me about it!  You're absolutely right.  Absolutely.  That's exactly how I feel.  Exactly.  I'm afraid I agree with James.  I have to side with Dad on this one.  No doubt about it.  (agree with the negative statement) Me neither.  (weak) I suppose so. /I guess so.  You have a point there.  I was just going to say that.

 I don't think so.  (strong) No way.  I'm afraid I disagree.  (strong) I totally disagree.  I beg to differ.  (strong) I'd say the exact opposite.  Not necessarily.  That's not always true.  That's not always the case.  No, I'm not so sure about that.

85a3d3acd7b32ade49b3.text: Moreover, there are situations when stating your reasons for agreeing or

693514a93468d77e75ec.text: disagreeing is necessary. It requires that you carefully consider arguments/evidence for and against the particular position or viewpoint raised in the material. Here are guide questions you can use.

bc3a069427a7655aa13e.text: 1. What are the strengths/advantages and weaknesses/disadvantages of _____________? 2. What evidence supports and contradicts ________________? 3. What are arguments for and counterarguments against ______________?

93675fb99001468b620a.text: In this age of technology, many young people obtain much of the information

eef7c69fd09131dde9e5.text: they need from online viewing materials. Such materials mostly come from Youtube, Instagram, and Snapchat—the most popular online platforms among teens based on a new Pew Research Center Survey (Anderson and Jiang, 2018).

896b0590e6cfa5a3b04f.text: As a student, you must enhance your capacity to filter information obtained from

2dc842198b96dbc05f28.text: such sources. It will make you avoid misinformation, which has recently become prevalent due to fake news. You also need to sharpen your skill in judging the relevance and worth of their content before using them as bases for personal decisions, especially when dealing with social issues, concerns in real life.

45a762da46a04cf9dc61.text: In making sound judgments about the overall quality of information presented

9727cda7ce339983488b.text: in a viewing material, you need to consider the following elements: 1. Relevance: the information's level of importance to a particular viewing

bc568e762acc2aa86b11.text: purpose or explicitly stated need for that information

f64363738acd61542fec.text: 2. Accuracy: the extent to which information contains factual and updated details that can be verified by consulting alternative and/or primary sources

522c4a003fe8db431a61.text: 3. Bias/Perspective: the position or slant toward which an author shapes information

770c6a737e89673e54d7.text: 4. Reliability: the information's level of trustworthiness based on information about the author and the publishing body

de5fa911c652d8a094a8.text: One essential skill we use in our day-to-day communication is listening. When

3a2a93bb535827107636.text: done right, we thoroughly understand matters we hear and come up with appropriate feedback when needed.

18a8b6ecc06aede27e8a.text: Effective listening requires the ability to evaluate whether we should believe a

bc02112ec8f83be830ca.text: point raised. It involves assessing the weight of the evidence used to support it.

7f55c2e26dde34388040.text:  In an argument, evidence refers to facts, documentation, or testimony used to strengthen a claim, support an argument or reach a conclusion. An argument is usually the main idea, often called a "claim" or "thesis statement," backed up with evidence that supports the idea.

8dde7ee078acf116538b.text: What are the types of evidence?

f579efbd9c1b23d1cec5.text: 1. Facts are a powerful means of convincing. They can come from reading, observation, or personal experience. Facts cannot be disputed, making them a strong form of evidence.

b6d791ef41072bb8e03d.text: Note: Do not confuse facts with truths. A "truth" is an idea believed by

98876afbc63dc4643235.text: many people, but it cannot be proven. For example: • Grass is green. • All cats are animals. • Jumping out of airplanes without a parachute is hazardous.

8e57eb99a55082f4f8d8.text: However, facts can be interpreted or presented in skewed ways,

d913e813fa3a8410956a.text: resulting in skewed or erroneous conclusions. Personal opinions, such as "Dustin Hoffman is the best actor who has ever lived," are never facts. They are claims. Examples:

8924b5c13253736000e6.text:  Grass is green. (in the winter?)  Stalin was a famous man, loved by many people.  It's a fact that the French are smelly and snobbish.

9fbe6fe47b7b81387bff.text: 2. Statistics provide excellent support for an argument. Arguments employing amounts and numbers are concrete and therefore support claims because they use logic and facts.

4a0ce46cd193674ffda0.text: Examples:  Over 61% of Americans are overweight.  As of January 28, 20201, there are already 518,407 confirmed COVID-

51c478c9ce9581e5d228.text: 3. Quotes from leading experts or authorities in their fields support a position. They serve as logical appeal and are accepted by other academics as an excellent way to back up claims.

1e6792322a495970a7fd.text:  Dr. Kenneth P. Moritsugu, U.S. Surgeon General, described the long term problems associated with underage drinking. Citing various studies, he said that "young people who start drinking before the age of 15 are five times more likely to have alcohol-related problems later in life."  Samantha King, a noted forensic specialist, stated that DNA evidence is usually indisputable.

fffd3e82ec5ebb215684.text: The authoritative information must be accurate and relevant to the point.

d470c8a7bdd7b5472292.text: 4. Examples or anecdotes from the writer's experience can enhance meaning and engage listeners. Personal examples make ideas concrete. These real-life examples allow listeners to relate to the issues personally.

da6760bfdef53614a481.text:  For many years, my best friend's husband beat her—the police did nothing about it; therefore, we need better laws so domestic abusers can be punished more stringently.

62ea58de74613d736ba8.text:  After living in Iceland for a decade, I can honestly say that the people there are kind and warm.

1e3fa05b1de1d2ac7821.text: However, for personal experience to be convincing, it must also be

26f748d726107cf93e79.text: applicable, present reasonable background understanding, show a universal or general situation, and be related to the thesis somehow.

2f3bee03960d99c89035.text: How are pieces of evidence evaluated?

fced23f53b0383b8c5ba.text: The following are guide questions in understanding evidence.

f6dda2dd5c85628b2808.text: 1. In what ways does this evidence support the assertion?

e596b73ccc6b537de68e.text: 2. How does the evidence relate to the original author's main idea? 3. Is there anything about the original author's main idea that can be applied to the assertion? 4. Is there anything about this quote or example that wouldn't be obvious to all readers? Is there anything unique or confusing about it?

d50cd85f7514aafea788.text: Example: Alcohol in many cultures plays a significant social role in many cultures. Still, most countries have laws that set the legal age to consume alcohol. However, the percentage of teenagers who drink alcohol is continuously increasing, resulting in various problems. Several studies reported that drinking alcohol during adolescence affects educational attainment by increasing the number of dropouts. This endangers the future of these children since it has been shown that underage drinking can cause alterations in the structure and function of the developing brains, which can impair learning. (Source: ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3026599)

2ccd685609444c3f77a4.text: Alcohol has negative effects on the educational attainment of adolescents.

12eb7e6088f5cd80f74d.text:  EVIDENCE  Several studies reported that drinking alcohol during adolescence affects

caaa21a712809440c221.text: educational attainment by increasing the number of dropouts.  Underage drinking can cause alterations in the structure and function of the developing brains, which can impair learning.

ff3a4c2e7fe86f0c119a.text: Likewise, identifying points/claims and evidence can also be used in materials listened to.

39a8059f12c9d0b86685.text: Listen to an excerpt from Priyanka Chopra’s speech on The Full Power of Women. Then, examine how the point/claim and evidence were identified.

8521676a25f60efff736.text: “My first experience of the glaring disparity between boys and girls came at a very, very young age… …I was seven or eight years old when my parents started taking me on these visits in a traveling clinic to developing communities around and villages around the city that we lived in called Bareilly. “..but the more I went on these expeditions, the more I began to notice the simplest things that distinguished a boy from a girl or man from a woman. For example, girls were pulled out of school when they hit puberty because they were considered ready for marriage and babies. That’s twelve and thirteen, while boys still enjoyed their childhood. Or basic human rights such as healthcare were denied just because they were women.” (Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iCwKM6uB71I ; starts at 2:51 and ends at 4:14)

558e44dbc7c414a476d7.text: CLAIM: Inequality between males and females is reflected even at a young age.

b20bbe30164762aa0723.text: EVIDENCE: “..girls were pulled out of school when they hit puberty because they were

bb72907f50ba2a71e480.text: considered ready for marriage and babies.” “..while boys still enjoyed their childhood.”

d819268c53cfb4eab00c.text: When analyzing pieces of evidence, we should tell how the author intended them to support the claim. Here are the steps in doing that: 1. Identify the point the author is trying to prove. 2. Identify specific facts, data, statistics, examples that support that point. 3. Explain how the pieces of evidence are supposed to relate to the claim. Example:  Statement: We should set a limit for our game time. In my experience, spending too much time on computer games prevents us from doing essential class works, making our grades suffer.  Point/Claim: We should set a limit for our game time.  Evidence: In my experience, spending too much time on computer games prevents us from doing essential class works, making our grades suffer.  Type of Evidence: Anecdotal evidence  Relation of the evidence to the point/claim: The evidence reflects the possible result of excessive online gaming, as experienced by the speaker. Note that even when the pieces of evidence are entirely accurate, there are other factors that we need to consider before using them as bases for our thoughts and actions. We need to ask the following questions:

342e05dd93af2a799eff.text: (Is the evidence enough, or do you need more to feel convinced?) Example:  It is going to rain because it is cloudy. (insufficient)  It will rain because it is cloudy, the barometer is dropping, the wind is picking up, and the air smells damp. (sufficient)

528ad3eff4c0ef3d0a2f.text: (Is the evidence really about the claim the author wants to prove. Or, did it go off tangent, providing facts that don't have anything to do with the claim/point?)

c5241af7d7adfa5d52b5.text: Example: I am shopping for a second-hand car and want to know if it is a good one.  The seller said that the car has a good paint job. (somewhat irrelevant when the concern is functionality.)  The seller said that the engine runs well and the transmission is in good condition. (relevant)

4b3028ef54373a38a032.text: (Does it accurately portray the subject, not distorted and just a select piece?) Example:  All Filipinos are helpful and generous, like Manny Pacquiao. (not representative of most, if not all, Filipinos.)

bd28584f5f63eab57024.text: Evidence evaluation is also important when dealing with listening materials. The

99efa1bd46415a2569ac.text: process will allow us to determine the value of what we have listened to in our lives.

c3a316a33c5bea8114c7.text: Listen to an excerpt from Emma Watson's speech on Gender Equality and analyze how the speech was analyzed and evaluated. You may refer to the transcript given below. “Men—I would like to take this opportunity to extend your formal invitation. Gender equality is your issue too. Because to date, I’ve seen my father’s role as a parent being valued less by society despite my needing his presence as a child as much as my mother’s. I’ve seen young men suffering from mental illness unable to ask for help for fear it would make them look less “macho”—in fact in the UK suicide is the biggest killer of men between 20-49 years of age; eclipsing road accidents, cancer and coronary heart disease. I’ve seen men made fragile and insecure by a distorted sense of what constitutes male success. Men don’t have the benefits of equality either. We don’t often talk about men being imprisoned by gender stereotypes but I can see that that they are and that when they are free, things will change for women as a natural consequence. If men don’t have to be aggressive in order to be accepted women won’t feel compelled to be submissive. If men don’t have to control, women won’t have to be controlled. Both men and women should feel free to be sensitive. Both men and women should feel free to be strong… It is time that we all perceive gender on a spectrum not as two opposing sets of ideals.” Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=l9FPp3YzjB4 ; starts at 5:12 and ends at 7:21

0369d6779054b157a69b.text: Point/Claim: Men don't have the benefits of equality either. Evidence: ".. I've seen my father's role as a parent being valued less by society despite

099ab83c388e12a51e6c.text: my needing his presence as a child as much as my mother's." "..young men suffering from mental illness unable to ask for help for fear it would make them look less "macho"—in fact in the UK suicide is the biggest killer of men between 20-49 years of age.."

d6a9e0ace1e8708967a4.text: Type of Evidence: Anecdotal and Statistical Evidence Relation of the evidence to the point/claim: Emma Watson provided adequate evidence to support her claim that gender equality is also a men’s issue—citing both

d4b1f4c6a48e898e8f35.text: statistical and anecdotal data. Aside from being sufficient, they are relevant to the central idea she conveyed.
